observation_summary: The MultivariateNormalDistribution.density(double[]) method returns incorrect values when the distribution dimension is odd, as evidenced by a failing test comparing it against a univariate normal distribution.
hypothesis: The density calculation algorithm for the multivariate normal distribution is likely using an incorrect formula or implementation detail when handling the determinant or the exponentiation part of the multivariate normal density function, specifically failing to account for the dimensionality correctly in the case of odd dimensions.
prediction: The code in MultivariateNormalDistribution.density() will likely contain a mathematical error in the calculation of the probability density function, such as an incorrect handling of the covariance matrix determinant or the exponent term, which manifests as a wrong result for odd-dimensional inputs.
experiment_rationale: The bug report explicitly states the method returns the wrong value for odd dimensions. Since the density function is a standard mathematical formula, the error must lie in the implementation of that formula (the algorithm) within the density method.
reasoning_summary: The defect is a computational error in the density function implementation. It is not a missing check (Checking), not a simple initialization error (Assignment/Initialization), and not a design-level capability gap (Function/Class/Object). It is a procedural error in the mathematical implementation, which falls squarely under Algorithm/Method.
evidence_used: The bug report title: 'MultivariateNormalDistribution.density(double[]) returns wrong value when the dimension is odd'
The failing test: 'org.apache.commons.math3.distribution.MultivariateNormalDistributionTest::testUnivariateDistribution' comparing univariate and multivariate density results.

alternative_types.why_not_primary: The issue is not a wrong constant or initialization, but a procedural error in the density calculation formula.
The capability exists, but the implementation of the algorithm is incorrect.
